blocks.text: The position and momentum of a particle cannot both be measured at the same time with perfect accuracy. There is always a fundamental uncertainty in any such measurement. It is not due to the measuring instrument but is a consequence of the wave-particle duality of matter and radiation. This was first proposed by Werner Heisenberg in 1927 and is known as Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. The uncertainty is negligible for the position and momentum of everyday objects but dominates in the atomic world: a stream of photons striking a flying tennis ball hardly affects its path, but one photon striking an electron drastically alters its motion.

Since light has wave properties, we can locate an electron only to within about one wavelength of the light used. To locate it with less uncertainty we must use light of shorter wavelength, but that alters its motion more, making the momentum measurement less precise. If light of wavelength lambda is used to locate a particle moving along the x-axis, the uncertainty in position is dx about lambda. At most the photon can transfer all its momentum h/lambda to the particle, whose momentum is then uncertain by dp about h/lambda. Multiplying, dx dp is about lambda (h/lambda) = h (18.14).

blocks.title: Position-momentum uncertainty principle
blocks.text: The product of the uncertainty dx in the position of a particle at some instant and the uncertainty dp in the x-component of its momentum at the same instant is approximately equal to Planck's constant h. Heisenberg's more careful calculation gives at best dx dp >= h-bar, where h-bar = h/(2 pi) = 1.05 x 10^-34 J s.

The uncertainty principle shows that electrons cannot exist inside the nucleus. A nucleus has a diameter of the order of 10^-15 m, so an electron inside would have a position uncertainty of about 10^-15 m and a momentum uncertainty dp about h/dx = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 10^-15 = 6.63 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1. The corresponding energy would be of the order of GeV (pc is about 1.2 GeV), far more than any electron in an atom has. So electrons do not exist inside the nucleus.

blocks.title: Units in the book
blocks.text: The book gives this momentum uncertainty as 6.63 x 10^-19 'J s'; momentum is measured in kg m s^-1 (equivalently N s).

Another form of the uncertainty principle relates the energy of a particle to the time for which it has that energy: dE dt is about h (18.15, 18.16), or at best dE dt >= h-bar. The more accurately we determine the energy of a particle, the more uncertain we are of the time during which it has that energy. Heisenberg received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1932 for his contribution to quantum physics. Because of this principle, every empirical measurement in the atomic world must have some uncertainty; in the sub-atomic world few things can be predicted with 100 per cent precision.

What can be the velocity of an electron enclosed in a box about the size of an atom, 1.0 x 10^-10 m? Solution: dp dx is about h, with dp about m dv, so dv = h/(m dx) = 6.63 x 10^-34 / (9.1 x 10^-31 x 1.0 x 10^-10) = 7.3 x 10^6 m s^-1.

Find the uncertainty in the energy of a photon emitted from an atom that radiates for about 10^-8 s. Solution: dE dt is about h, so dE = h/dt = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 10^-8 = 6.63 x 10^-26 J. In electron volts, dE = 6.63 x 10^-26 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 4 x 10^-7 eV.

blocks.prompt: Why is the uncertainty principle unimportant for a cricket ball but important for an electron?
blocks.explanation: Because h is tiny: for a heavy ball the resulting uncertainty in velocity (h/(m dx)) is far too small to notice, but for an electron of tiny mass confined to atomic distances the velocity uncertainty is millions of metres per second.

items: Uncertainty principle (Heisenberg, 1927): dx dp is about h (at best >= h/2 pi).
Energy-time form: dE dt is about h.
Electrons cannot be inside the nucleus; measurements at atomic scale always carry uncertainty.
